Subject: Order form: dispute lanes + urgent remedy language (ACME)

Hi Rishi,

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. Our GC team (copied) asked us to flag a handful of redlines on the Order Form and MSA relating to governing law and injunctive relief. Attached is a clean redline of the Order Form with the suggested changes (ACME_OrderForm_redline_1010.docx). Key asks:

- ACME wants governing law and seat to be Delaware.
- They insist on an explicit carveout allowing courts to grant injunctive relief (IP/data preservation) without needing to go to arbitration first.
- They also request an exclusive covenant that, for emergency injunctive relief, venue will be the courts in NY.

Can you confirm whether Redwood can accept a limited court carveout for emergency injunctive relief (narrowly tailored to IP/data exfiltration and preservation) while keeping arbitration for the rest? If so, what seat do we propose for arbitration and governing law?

From the commercial side, they may push for a single jurisdiction to avoid forum shopping — happy to connect with your team.

Best,

Kimberly / Laura — forwarding ACME's redline. Copying Mark from their team. Quick context: ACME is pushing for Delaware law + exclusive NY courts for emergency injunctive relief — wanting a carveout from arbitration for IP/data preservation. Commercial is okay with a narrow carve but wants to avoid opening broad litigation paths.

My questions for legal:
- Can we accept an injunctive relief carve limited to (i) injunctive relief to stop imminent data exfiltration or IP misappropriation and (ii) preservation orders, without opening up general disputes to court?
- If we agree to a carve, do we need to specify that the court request is only for temporary relief and that final remedies remain under arbitration?
- What's our preferred governing law and arbitral seat that balances enforcement and customer's commercial asks?

Proposed next step: Kimberly to propose language we can send back as Redwood's counter. Laura, can you advise on enforcement risk / precedent?

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura_bennett@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 11 Oct 2028 09:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Fwd: Order form: dispute lanes + urgent remedy language (ACME)

Rishi / Laura — reviewed ACME's redline and drafted a compromise redline (attached). Key points from legal:

1) Injunctive relief / interim measures
- We can accept a narrowly tailored court carveout for "interim injunctive relief to preserve the status quo (including preservation of data, emergency injunctive relief to prevent immediate data exfiltration, and to protect intellectual property)".
- The carveout should be limited in scope and duration: courts may grant interim relief only until the arbitrator can address the merits unless the court expressly finds irreparable harm that justifies longer relief.
- Add an obligation to use expedited arbitration procedures for merit determination where a court issues interim relief (to avoid long dual-track litigation).

2) Governing law vs seat
- Governing law: propose California state law (no substantive difference for enforcement vs Delaware in most of our contracts; CA is familiar for our litigation team).
- Arbitration seat: San Francisco (neutral, convenient for Redwood and many US counterparties).
- If the customer insists on Delaware law, consider Delaware law with SF seat as a balanced permutation.

3) Emergency forum specificity
- Resist exclusive venue language pointing to NY courts. Instead propose that the court with "competent jurisdiction" can grant interim relief and expressly exclude forum-selection for final remedies (final remedies governed by arbitration). This avoids giving the customer exclusive control over forum for final relief.

4) Enforcement risk / practicality
- Laura, please confirm whether CA law materially changes our exposure on IP injunctions vs DE. My read: similar standards for preliminary injunctive relief (irreparable harm, inadequate remedy at law, balance of equities, public interest).

I attached: Redwood_proposed_redline_20281011.docx — includes: (a) a 7-day emergency notice requirement to Redwood before seeking a court order where feasible; (b) language requiring the party seeking emergency relief to include a brief showing as to why arbitration cannot provide adequate immediate relief.

If this looks okay commercially, Rishi, we'll send this back as Redwood's counter.

Kimberly Park
Head of Contracts & Compliance
Redwood Inference

Attachments: Redwood_proposed_redline_20281011.docx

Thanks Rishi and Kimberly — appreciate the quick review and thoughtful compromise language. ACME's GC reviewed and provided a short counter (attached). Their positions:

- ACME will consider your proposed narrow carve for injunctive relief but wants the governing law to remain Delaware.
- They propose an explicit list of courts for interim relief (NY or DE courts) to avoid uncertainty.
- They also asked whether Redwood will accept a short, unilateral emergency-order right (i.e., seeker can file ex parte if necessary) — they say it's essential in some operational contexts.

We attached ACME_counter_1011.pdf with markups. Short-term ask: can you confirm whether Redwood will accept: (1) Delaware law + (2) the narrow injunctive carve with language that interim relief can be sought in NY or DE courts but final remedies go to arbitration?

If Redwood needs a small commercial concession to accept DE law, let us know and we can run that up.

Regards,
Sarah Lin
Senior Counsel, Contracts
ACME Cloud

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi_malhotra@redwood.com>

Date: Thu, 12 Oct 2028 09:05:00 -0700
Subject: Internal: ACME redlines — recommended commercial offset and final position

Team — summary and recommended path:

- Legal's compromise (see Kimberly's redline) looks sound and defensible.
- Commercial: ACME prefers Delaware law. To close quickly, suggest offering a one‑time onboarding credit of 5% on year one committed spend in exchange for Redwood accepting Delaware law (with SF arbitration seat).
- Ask Kimberly: if we accept Delaware law (instead of CA), any material change to injunctive relief carve or enforcement risk? Laura, please flag any case law concerns.

If legal can confirm that Redwood's narrow injunctive carve + requirement for expedited arbitration is acceptable under Delaware law, we should propose:
1) Governing law: Delaware;
2) Arbitration seat: San Francisco (administrative convenience);
3) Interim injunctive relief: courts in NY or DE may issue temporary relief limited to preservation/IP/data exfiltration; final disposition of claims remains in arbitration;
4) Add expedited arbitration trigger and 7-day notice when practicable.

If all agree, Kimberly please send the counter with the commercial offset and I'll run the commercial concession with ACME.

Thanks —
Rishi
Senior Director, Sales — Enterprise
